questions.title: Custom Exception Hierarchy
questions.objective: Define base AppError and subclasses ValidationError and AuthError.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Build your own exception classes, so one except clause can catch a whole family of errors.
• class AppError(Exception) with a class attribute code = 500
• class ValidationError(AppError) with code = 400
• class AuthError(AppError) with code = 401

Write a class UserStore that keeps usernames and passwords:
• register(self, user, pwd): raise ValidationError('password too short') if pwd has fewer than 6 characters, raise ValidationError('user exists') if the user is already registered, otherwise store the user
• login(self, user, pwd): raise AuthError('invalid credentials') if the user is unknown or the password is wrong

Commands:
• REGISTER user pwd → print REGISTERED user
• LOGIN user pwd → print WELCOME user
• For both commands, catch AppError (the BASE class) and print <ClassName>[<code>]: <message>, for example ValidationError[400]: user exists

Example: REGISTER asha secret1, LOGIN asha nope prints REGISTERED asha and AuthError[401]: invalid credentials.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
User names and passwords are words without spaces
sample_inputs:
2
REGISTER asha secret1
LOGIN asha nope
hints: class ValidationError(AppError): code = 400 is a complete class: it inherits everything else from AppError.
except AppError as e: also catches ValidationError and AuthError, because they are subclasses.
type(e).__name__ gives the class name, and e.code finds the class attribute of the subclass.

questions.title: Vehicle Hierarchy with Super
questions.objective: Implement Vehicle base and Car subclass extending __init__ via super().
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write three classes that build on each other with super():
• Vehicle: __init__(self, make, model, year) stores the three values. Class attribute wheels = 0. describe(self) returns '<year> <make> <model>'
• Car(Vehicle): __init__(self, make, model, year, doors) calls super().__init__(make, model, year) and stores doors. Class attribute wheels = 4. describe(self) returns super().describe() + ' (<doors> doors)'
• ElectricCar(Car): __init__(self, make, model, year, doors, kwh) calls super().__init__(...) and stores kwh. describe(self) returns super().describe() + ' [<kwh> kWh]'

Commands:
• VEHICLE make model year, CAR make model year doors, ECAR make model year doors kwh → create the object and keep it in a list (prints nothing)
• LIST → print describe() of every object in creation order
• INFO i → for the object at index i (from 0) print: <ClassName>, wheels=<wheels>, is Car: <True/False>. Use isinstance(obj, Car)

Example: CAR Toyota Corolla 2020 4 then LIST prints 2020 Toyota Corolla (4 doors).
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description). INFO always uses a valid index.
questions.output_format: LIST prints one line per object; INFO prints one line. Create commands print nothing.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
Makes and models are words without spaces
year, doors and kwh are integers
hints: super().__init__(make, model, year) lets Vehicle set the shared attributes, so Car does not repeat that code.
ElectricCar inherits wheels = 4 from Car without writing it again.
isinstance(obj, Car) is True for an ElectricCar too, because ElectricCar is a subclass of Car.

questions.title: Dataclass with Ordering
questions.objective: Implement @dataclass(order=True) for items comparing by price.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: The dataclasses module writes __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and, with order=True, also <, <=, > and >= for you.

Write a dataclass Item:
@dataclass(order=True)
class Item:
price: float
name: str

Comparisons use the fields in the order they are written: first price, then name (only when the prices are equal).

Commands:
• ADD name price → create an Item and keep it in a list (prints nothing)
• SORTED → print the items from cheapest to most expensive, one per line, using repr (the dataclass repr, like Item(price=2.5, name='pen'))
• CHEAPEST → print min(items) using repr
• COMPARE i j → compare the items at indexes i and j (from 0) and print <, == or >

Example: ADD pen 2.5, ADD book 12.0, CHEAPEST prints Item(price=2.5, name='pen').
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description). SORTED, CHEAPEST and COMPARE are only used when the list has the items they need.
questions.output_format: SORTED prints one line per item; CHEAPEST and COMPARE print one line. ADD prints nothing.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
Names are words without spaces
0 <= price <= 10^6
sample_inputs:
4
ADD b 5
ADD a 5
SORTED
COMPARE 0 1
hints: from dataclasses import dataclass, then put @dataclass(order=True) on the line above class Item.
Create items with Item(float(price), name): the fields come in the order they are declared.
sorted(items) and min(items) work directly, because order=True gives the class comparison methods.

questions.title: Employee Payroll Polymorphism
questions.objective: Base Employee with Salaried and Hourly polymorphic earnings.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Polymorphism means different classes answer the same method call in their own way.

Write a base class and two subclasses:
• Employee: __init__(self, name). monthly_pay(self) raises NotImplementedError, because a plain Employee has no pay rule
• Salaried(Employee): __init__(self, name, annual). monthly_pay returns annual / 12
• Hourly(Employee): __init__(self, name, rate, hours). monthly_pay returns rate * hours for the first 160 hours, plus 1.5 * rate for every hour above 160

Commands:
• SALARIED name annual, HOURLY name rate hours → create the employee (prints nothing)
• PAYROLL → print one line per employee in creation order: <name> (<ClassName>): <pay with 2 decimals>, then a last line TOTAL: <sum with 2 decimals>. The loop must just call e.monthly_pay() for every employee, without checking the type

Example: SALARIED asha 60000, HOURLY ben 20 170, PAYROLL prints
asha (Salaried): 5000.00
ben (Hourly): 3500.00
TOTAL: 8500.00
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: For every PAYROLL: one line per employee, then the TOTAL line.
hints: Call super().__init__(name) in both subclasses.
Overtime hours are max(0, hours - 160); normal hours are min(hours, 160).
The PAYROLL loop calls employee.monthly_pay() and Python picks the right version for each object.

test_cases.input:

HOURLY x 12.5 40
PAYROLL
SALARIED y 12
PAYROLL

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
extra_fields.output_format: For every PAYROLL: one line per employee, then the TOTAL line.

questions.title: Payment Gateway Polymorphism
questions.objective: Abstract PaymentGateway with CreditCard, UPI, and Crypto classes.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: An abstract class describes what every subclass must provide, and cannot be created itself.

Write the classes using the abc module:
• PaymentGateway(ABC) with an abstract method fee(self, amount), and a normal method pay(self, amount) that returns (amount + fee, fee)
• CreditCard: fee = 2.9% of the amount + 0.30
• UPI: fee = 0
• Crypto: fee = 1.00 + 1% of the amount

Commands:
• PAY method amount → method is CARD, UPI or CRYPTO. Print <ClassName>: charged <total> (fee <fee>), both with 2 decimals. If the amount <= 0 print INVALID AMOUNT. If the method is unknown print UNKNOWN METHOD
• ABSTRACT → try to create PaymentGateway() directly. Python raises TypeError because it has an abstract method: catch it and print CANNOT INSTANTIATE PaymentGateway

Example: PAY CARD 100 prints CreditCard: charged 103.20 (fee 3.20).
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
hints: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod; put @abstractmethod above def fee.
Keep a dictionary {'CARD': CreditCard(), 'UPI': UPI(), 'CRYPTO': Crypto()} to pick the gateway.
pay() is written once in the base class and calls self.fee(amount), which runs the subclass version.

questions.title: Shape Geometry Polymorphism
questions.objective: Base Shape with Circle and Polygon computing polymorphic area.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a base class Shape and two subclasses:
• Shape: area(self) raises NotImplementedError
• Circle(Shape): __init__(self, r); area = math.pi * r * r
• Polygon(Shape): __init__(self, points) with a list of (x, y) tuples. If there are fewer than 3 points, raise ValueError('polygon needs at least 3 points'). Area with the shoelace formula: abs(sum of x[i] * y[i+1] - x[i+1] * y[i] over all i, wrapping around to the first point) / 2

Commands:
• CIRCLE r → add a circle (prints nothing)
• POLYGON x1 y1 x2 y2 ... → add a polygon. If it raises ValueError, print INVALID: <message> and do not add it
• LIST → one line per shape in the order added: <ClassName>: <area with 2 decimals>
• TOTAL → the sum of all areas with 2 decimals
• LARGEST → <ClassName>: <area> of the shape with the biggest area (the first one on a tie), or NONE if there are no shapes

Example: CIRCLE 1, POLYGON 0 0 4 0 4 3, LIST prints Circle: 3.14 and Polygon: 6.00.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One line for every TOTAL, LARGEST and rejected POLYGON; one line per shape for every LIST.
sample_outputs:
INVALID: polygon needs at least 3 points
NONE
hints: Pair the coordinates with zip: list(zip(nums[0::2], nums[1::2])).
In the shoelace sum, the next point of the last point is the first one: points[(i + 1) % n].
max(shapes, key=lambda s: s.area()) returns the first shape with the largest area.

questions.title: Sequence Magic Methods
questions.objective: Implement __len__ and __getitem__ to enable indexing and slicing.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: When a class defines __len__ and __getitem__, Python lets you use len(obj), obj[i] and obj[a:b] on it, like on a list.

Write a class SongList that wraps a list of song names:
• __init__(self, songs=None) stores a copy of the list (an empty list when songs is None)
• add(self, song) appends a song
• __len__(self) returns the number of songs
• __getitem__(self, index): if index is a slice object, return a NEW SongList with the selected songs; otherwise return the song at that index. A bad index raises IndexError by itself
• __repr__(self) returns SongList(<list of songs>)

Commands:
• ADD song → add a song (the song name is one word; prints nothing)
• LEN → print len(songs)
• GET i → print songs[i], or INDEX ERROR if it raises IndexError
• SLICE a b [step] → print repr(songs[a:b]) or repr(songs[a:b:step]) when a step is given

Example: ADD a, ADD b, ADD c, GET -1, SLICE 0 2 prints c and SongList(['a', 'b']).
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every LEN, GET and SLICE command.
sample_inputs:

ADD a
ADD b
ADD c
GET -1
SLICE 0 2
hints: isinstance(index, slice) tells you whether obj[a:b] was used.
self.songs[index] already understands both ints and slices; just wrap a slice result in SongList(...).
Python turns songs[0:2] into songs.__getitem__(slice(0, 2, None)).

questions.title: Value Equality & Hashing
questions.objective: Implement __eq__ and __hash__ for hash table compatibility in sets/dicts.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: By default two objects are equal only if they are the SAME object. To use objects as set items or dict keys by their VALUE, a class needs __eq__ and a matching __hash__: equal objects must have equal hashes.

Write a class Point:
• __init__(self, x, y)
• __eq__(self, other): True when other is a Point with the same x and y. For anything else return NotImplemented
• __hash__(self): return hash((self.x, self.y))
• __repr__(self): Point(x, y)

Commands:
• ADD x y → add Point(x, y) to a set. Print ADDED, or DUPLICATE if an equal point is already there
• HAS x y → print True or False (is an equal point in the set?)
• COUNT → print the size of the set
• LABEL x y name → store name in a dict under the key Point(x, y) (a new name replaces the old one; prints nothing)
• NAME x y → print the label of Point(x, y), or NONE

Example: ADD 1 2, ADD 1 2, COUNT prints ADDED, DUPLICATE, 1.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every ADD, HAS, COUNT and NAME command.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
-10^9 <= x, y <= 10^9 (integers)
Labels are words without spaces
hints: Without __hash__, defining __eq__ makes the class unhashable, so it cannot go in a set.
Hashing the tuple (x, y) gives equal points equal hashes.
Point(1, 2) in points calls __hash__ first, then __eq__ to confirm the match.

LABEL 0 0 b

COUNT

Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).

questions.title: Fraction Arithmetic Dunders
questions.objective: Implement __add__, __sub__, and __mul__ on Fraction with GCD reduction.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a class Frac for exact fractions (do not use the fractions module):
• __init__(self, num, den): if den is 0 raise ZeroDivisionError('zero denominator'). Store the fraction in lowest terms: divide both by math.gcd(num, den), and keep the sign in the numerator (the denominator is always positive)
• __add__, __sub__ and __mul__ each return a NEW Frac
a/b + c/d = (a*d + c*b) / (b*d), a/b - c/d = (a*d - c*b) / (b*d), a/b * c/d = (a*c) / (b*d)
• __str__ returns 'num/den', or just 'num' when den is 1

Each input line is one expression: <fraction> <op> <fraction>, where a fraction is written num/den and op is +, - or *. Print the result with str(). If creating a fraction raises ZeroDivisionError, print ERROR: zero denominator.

Examples: 1/2 + 1/3 → 5/6, 2/4 * 2/1 → 1, 1/0 + 1/2 → ERROR: zero denominator.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of expressions Q.
Next Q lines: <num>/<den> <op> <num>/<den>, separated by spaces.
questions.output_format: Q lines: the result, or ERROR: zero denominator.
hints: math.gcd always returns a non-negative number; math.gcd(0, 5) is 5, so 0/5 becomes 0/1.
If den < 0 after reducing, multiply both num and den by -1.
a + b on two Frac objects calls a.__add__(b).

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the number of expressions Q.
Next Q lines: <num>/<den> <op> <num>/<den>, separated by spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: Q lines: the result, or ERROR: zero denominator.

questions.title: Diamond MRO Inspection
questions.objective: Demonstrate method resolution order (__mro__) across diamond hierarchy.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In a diamond hierarchy, two classes inherit from the same base, and a fourth class inherits from both. Python decides the lookup order with the MRO (method resolution order), and super() follows that order.

Write these classes. Every hello(self) returns its own class name, followed by ' -> ' and super().hello(), except Base, which just returns 'Base':
• Base
• Left(Base)
• Right(Base)
• Child(Left, Right)
• Child2(Right, Left)

Commands (ClassName is one of the five names):
• MRO ClassName → print the names in ClassName.__mro__ joined with ' -> ' (this includes object at the end)
• CALL ClassName → print ClassName().hello()
• If the class name is not one of the five, print UNKNOWN CLASS

Examples: CALL Child prints Child -> Left -> Right -> Base. Base runs only once, even though two classes inherit from it.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
sample_outputs:
Child -> Left -> Right -> Base
Child -> Left -> Right -> Base -> object
hints: Keep the classes in a dictionary by name: {'Base': Base, 'Left': Left, ...}.
Each class's __name__ attribute gives its name: [c.__name__ for c in cls.__mro__].
super().hello() in Left calls Right.hello() when the object is a Child: super() follows the MRO of the object, not the parent written in the class.

Child -> Left -> Right -> Base -> object

Child2 -> Right -> Left -> Base -> object
Child2 -> Right -> Left -> Base

questions.title: Property Decorator Validation
questions.objective: Use @property and @setter to enforce validation on private attribute.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A property looks like a normal attribute from outside, but runs your code when it is read or assigned. That lets a class reject bad values.

Write a class Product:
• __init__(self, name, price) stores the name in a read-only property and assigns self.price = price, so the setter checks the starting price too
• The real value is kept in self._price (the underscore means "private")
• @property price returns self._price
• @price.setter: if the value is negative, raise ValueError('price cannot be negative'); otherwise store it
• @property name returns self._name, with NO setter, so obj.name = ... raises AttributeError
• apply_discount(self, pct): if pct is not between 0 and 100, raise ValueError('discount must be 0-100'); otherwise self.price = self.price * (1 - pct / 100)

The first line creates the product. If that raises ValueError, print ERROR: <message> and stop. Commands:
• GET → print <name>: <price with 2 decimals>
• SET p → assign product.price = p
• DISCOUNT pct → call apply_discount
• RENAME new → try product.name = new
For SET, DISCOUNT and RENAME print OK, or ERROR: <message> for ValueError, or ERROR: read-only for AttributeError.

Example: product pen 10, then SET -5, DISCOUNT 50, GET prints ERROR: price cannot be negative, OK, pen: 5.00.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the product name and the starting price.
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: ERROR: <message> if the product cannot be created. Otherwise one output line for every command.
sample_outputs:
ERROR: price cannot be negative
OK
pen: 5.00
hints: The setter method has the same name as the property: @price.setter then def price(self, value).
Inside the class, assign self.price = ..., not self._price = ..., so every change goes through the check.
A property without a setter raises AttributeError when you assign to it.

test_cases.output:

OK
pen: 5.00

ERROR: discount must be 0-100
ERROR: discount must be 0-100
OK
lamp: 0.00

DISCOUNT 25
RENAME seat
SET -0.01
GET

Line 1: the number of commands Q.

questions.title: State Pattern Workflow
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In the State pattern, every state is its own class, and the object hands each action to its current state. A state either returns the next state or refuses the action.

Order life cycle:
• DRAFT --pay--> PAID --ship--> SHIPPED --deliver--> DELIVERED
• cancel is allowed from DRAFT and PAID and leads to CANCELLED
• Every other action is not allowed

Write:
• class InvalidTransition(Exception)
• class State with name = 'STATE' and methods pay, ship, deliver and cancel that all raise InvalidTransition(f'cannot {action} when {self.name}')
• One subclass per state (Draft, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled) with its own name in capitals, overriding ONLY the actions it allows; each allowed action returns the next state object
• class Order with self.state = Draft() and a method do(self, action) that calls the matching method of the state and stores the returned state

Commands:
• PAY, SHIP, DELIVER, CANCEL → print the new state's name, or INVALID: <message>
• STATUS → print the current state's name

Example: PAY, DELIVER, SHIP prints PAID, INVALID: cannot deliver when PAID, SHIPPED.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
sample_outputs:
PAID
INVALID: cannot deliver when PAID
SHIPPED

DRAFT

questions.title: Context Manager Dunders
questions.objective: Implement __enter__ and __exit__ for resource acquisition and error suppression.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A with statement calls __enter__ when the block starts and __exit__ when it ends, even if the block raises an error. If __exit__ returns True, the error is suppressed (swallowed); otherwise it continues outward.

Write a class Resource:
• Class attribute open_count = 0 (how many resources are open right now)
• __init__(self, name) stores the name
• __enter__(self): add 1 to Resource.open_count, print acquire <name>, return self
• __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb): subtract 1 from Resource.open_count and print release <name>. If exc_type is ValueError, print suppressed ValueError: <message> and return True. For any other error (or none), return False

Commands:
• USE name OK → with Resource(name): print working <name>
• USE name VALUE → with Resource(name): raise ValueError('bad value')
• USE name KEY → with Resource(name): raise KeyError('missing')
• An error that is not suppressed reaches the driver: catch it there and print unhandled <ExceptionName>
• OPEN → print Resource.open_count

Example: USE db VALUE prints acquire db, release db, suppressed ValueError: bad value.

Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: USE <name> <OK|VALUE|KEY> or OPEN.
questions.output_format: The lines printed by the resource and the driver, in order.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
Names are words without spaces
sample_outputs:

release db
suppressed ValueError: bad value

acquire file
working file
release file
0
hints: issubclass(exc_type, ValueError) is safe only when exc_type is not None; exc_type is None when the block ended normally.
Returning True from __exit__ tells Python the error was handled.
Wrap the with statement in try / except Exception as e in the driver to catch what __exit__ let through.

questions.title: In-Memory Command Undo/Redo
questions.objective: Implement Command pattern with .execute() and .undo() on text document.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In the Command pattern every change is an object that knows how to do AND undo itself. An editor keeps the done commands on an undo stack, and undone commands on a redo stack.

Write:
• class Document with self.text = ''
• class AppendCommand(doc, text): execute adds text to the end; undo removes it again
• class DeleteCommand(doc, n): execute removes the last n characters (or all of them if there are fewer) and REMEMBERS what it removed; undo puts that text back
• class Editor:
- run(command): command.execute(), push it on the undo stack and CLEAR the redo stack
- undo(): pop from the undo stack, call undo(), push on the redo stack. Returns False when there is nothing to undo
- redo(): pop from the redo stack, call execute() again, push on the undo stack. Returns False when there is nothing to redo

Commands:
• APPEND text → the text is everything after 'APPEND ' (it may contain spaces); prints nothing
• DELETE n → prints nothing
• UNDO → prints nothing, or NOTHING TO UNDO
• REDO → prints nothing, or NOTHING TO REDO
• SHOW → print the text between square brackets, for example [hello world]

Example: APPEND hello, APPEND world, DELETE 3, SHOW, UNDO, SHOW prints [hello wo] and [hello world].
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each. For APPEND, the text starts right after the first space.
questions.output_format: One line for every SHOW, and NOTHING TO UNDO / NOTHING TO REDO when those commands cannot run.
questions.constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
0 <= n <= 1000
1 <= length of appended text <= 100
sample_inputs:

APPEND  world
DELETE 3
SHOW
UNDO
SHOW

hints: AppendCommand.undo can cut len(self.text) characters off the end: doc.text = doc.text[:-len(self.text)].
DeleteCommand.execute: self.removed = doc.text[len(doc.text) - k:] with k = min(n, len(doc.text)).
Use line[7:] (everything after 'APPEND ') so that spaces inside the text are kept.

questions.title: Classmethod Alternative Constructors
questions.objective: Use @classmethod factories and @staticmethod helpers, and see cls work for subclasses.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A @classmethod receives the class itself as cls, so it can build objects in other ways than __init__ ("alternative constructors"). Because it calls cls(...), a subclass that uses it gets an object of the SUBCLASS. A @staticmethod receives neither self nor cls; it is a plain helper that belongs to the class.

Write:
• class Date with __init__(self, year, month, day)
• @staticmethod is_leap(year): divisible by 4 and not by 100, or divisible by 400
• @staticmethod is_valid(year, month, day): month 1-12, day from 1 to the length of that month (February has 29 days in a leap year)
• @classmethod from_string(cls, text): text is YYYY-MM-DD. If it does not have three numeric parts, or is_valid is False, raise ValueError('invalid date'). Otherwise return cls(year, month, day)
• __str__ returns YYYY-MM-DD (year with 4 digits, month and day with 2 digits)
• class EuroDate(Date) that only overrides __str__ to return DD/MM/YYYY

Commands:
• PARSE text → print Date.from_string(text)
• PARSE_EU text → print EuroDate.from_string(text) and its class name: <date> (EuroDate)
• LEAP year → print Date.is_leap(year)
• For a ValueError print INVALID DATE

Example: PARSE 2024-02-29 prints 2024-02-29, and PARSE_EU 2024-03-05 prints 05/03/2024 (EuroDate).

Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
hints: Inside from_string, text.split('-') must give exactly 3 parts that are all digits.
f'{self.month:02d}' writes the month with a leading zero.

questions.title: Rich Comparisons with total_ordering
questions.objective: Define __eq__ and __lt__ and let functools.total_ordering supply the rest.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: functools.total_ordering fills in <=, > and >= when a class defines __eq__ and ONE ordering method such as __lt__.

Write a class Version for version strings like 1.2.10:
• __init__(self, text) stores the text and a tuple of ints. Remove zeros at the END of the tuple, so 1.0 and 1.0.0 are the same version (but keep at least one part)
• __eq__ compares the tuples (return NotImplemented for non-Version objects)
• __lt__ compares the tuples (tuples compare item by item, so (1, 10) > (1, 2))
• __hash__ returns hash of the tuple, so equal versions have equal hashes
• __repr__ returns the original text
• Decorate the class with @total_ordering

Commands:
• CMP a b → print a < b, a == b, a > b, a <= b as four words True/False separated by spaces
• SORT v1 v2 ... → print the versions sorted from oldest to newest (equal versions keep their input order), separated by spaces
• MAX v1 v2 ... → print the newest version (the first one if several are equal)
• UNIQUE v1 v2 ... → print the number of different versions (use a set)

Example: CMP 1.2 1.10 prints True False False True.

Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
questions.output_format: One output line for every command, as described.

1 <= Q <= 1000
Versions have 1 to 10 numeric parts separated by dots
Each part is between 0 and 10^9
hints: from functools import total_ordering, then @total_ordering above the class.
while len(parts) > 1 and parts[-1] == 0: parts.pop() removes trailing zeros.
sorted() is stable, so equal versions stay in their input order.

questions.title: Mixin Composition
questions.objective: Add reusable behaviour to unrelated classes with mixins and multiple inheritance.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A mixin is a small class that adds one ability and is meant to be combined with other classes through multiple inheritance.

Write two mixins:
• JsonMixin.to_json(self): return json.dumps of the object's attributes (vars(self)) with sort_keys=True
• EqualityMixin.__eq__(self, other): two objects are equal when they have the SAME class and the same attributes (vars). Return NotImplemented for objects of another class

And two unrelated classes that use them:
• class User(JsonMixin, EqualityMixin) with __init__(self, name, email)
• class Product(JsonMixin) with __init__(self, title, price) (price is an int). Product does NOT use EqualityMixin

Commands:
• USER name email, PRODUCT title price → create the object and keep it in a list (prints nothing)
• JSON i → print objects[i].to_json()
• SAME i j → print objects[i] == objects[j]. Products have only the default equality, so two different Product objects are never equal, even with the same data
• MIXINS i → print the class name, then the mixins it has, as <ClassName>: <mixins> where the mixins are JsonMixin and/or EqualityMixin (in that order, separated by a comma and a space) found with isinstance()

Example: USER asha a@x.io, JSON 0 prints {"email": "a@x.io", "name": "asha"}.

questions.title: LRU Cache Container
questions.objective: Build an LRU cache with __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__, __contains__ and __len__.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A Least Recently Used (LRU) cache holds at most capacity items. When it is full and a new key arrives, it removes the item that was used longest ago.

Write a class LRUCache that behaves like a dictionary through magic methods. Store the items in a collections.OrderedDict, oldest first:
• __init__(self, capacity)
• __setitem__(self, key, value): store the value and mark the key as most recently used (move_to_end). If the cache now has more than capacity items, remove the oldest one (popitem(last=False)) and remember its key in self.last_evicted (otherwise set self.last_evicted = None)
• __getitem__(self, key): return the value and mark the key as most recently used. A missing key raises KeyError
• __delitem__(self, key): remove the key (KeyError if missing)
• __contains__(self, key): True/False, WITHOUT changing the order
• __len__(self): the number of items
• __repr__(self): LRUCache([key1, key2, ...]) with the keys from oldest to newest, written as a Python list

The first line gives the capacity. Commands:
• PUT key value → cache[key] = value, then print OK, or OK (evicted <key>)
• GET key → print cache[key], or MISS
• HAS key → print key in cache
• DEL key → del cache[key] and print OK, or MISS
• LEN → print len(cache)
• SHOW → print repr(cache)

Example with capacity 2: PUT a 1, PUT b 2, GET a, PUT c 3 prints OK, OK, 1, OK (evicted b). Reading a made b the oldest.

Line 1: the number of commands Q.

Updating an existing key also makes it the newest, and never evicts anything.
Write the driver with cache[key], key in cache, del cache[key] and len(cache): Python calls your magic methods.
